1	// V-register transport staging: the host<->guest-RAM half of the V data
2	// regfile transfer. The Debug Module abstract-command space has no slots for
3	// v0..v31 (the RISC-V Debug Spec leaves V to the Program Buffer or
4	// implementation-specific extensions), so vsim moves v0..v31 by executing a
5	// vle8.v/vse8.v sweep on the halted hart through the Program Buffer (see
6	// pb_v_data_sweep in program_buffer.hpp, driven by ResumeDriver on resume and
7	// StateDrain at drain). That sweep loads/stores the V scratch region of guest
8	// RAM -- the top page of the mapped span (v_scratch_gpa, L26); this header
9	// provides the matching host-side copy:
10	//
11	//   - stage_v_to_scratch: state.vreg[] -> scratch RAM, called before resume so
12	//     the ResumeDriver vle8.v sweep reads QEMU 1's V values.
13	//   - read_v_from_scratch: scratch RAM -> state.vreg[], called after the
14	//     StateDrain vse8.v sweep so the drained v0..v31 land in state.vreg[]
15	//     (the handoff file).
16	//
17	// The transfer is transparent to the workload: benchmark binaries issue no
18	// transport code, only the enter_vsim / exit_vsim markers. rt_c_v_regs.c is
19	// the reference fixture.
20	//
21	// Pure logic: no SystemC, no DMI bus. Easy to unit-test.
22	
23	#pragma once
24	
25	#include "hybrid/state_abi.h"
26	
27	#include <cstddef>
28	#include <cstdint>
29	#include <cstring>
30	#include <span>
31	#include <stdexcept>
32	
33	namespace hybrid
34	{
35	
36	// Total scratch bytes needed: 32 V regs × HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX. Sized to the
37	// maximum supported VLEN; the actual per-reg byte count is `vlenb`. Defined in
38	// the shared ABI (HYBRID_V_SCRATCH_BYTES) so the driver's mmap sizing and this
39	// consumer agree on one count (L26/F2).
40	inline constexpr std::size_t kVScratchBytes = HYBRID_V_SCRATCH_BYTES;
41	
42	// L26: the scratch region is the TOP kVScratchBytes of the mapped RAM span,
43	// not a fixed address. Scheme D parks it just above the program's declared
44	// RAM (the driver maps one page more than --mem-size), so no program layout
45	// can collide with it. This is the single source of truth for the GUEST
46	// address the Program-Buffer sweep (ResumeDriver/StateDrain) loads/stores
47	// through; the host stager below copies span-relative and needs no base.
48	inline constexpr auto v_scratch_gpa(uint64_t ram_base, std::size_t ram_size)
49	  -> uint64_t
50	{
51	  return ram_base + static_cast<uint64_t>(ram_size) - kVScratchBytes;
52	}
53	
54	// Sentinel for "no V scratch configured". ResumeDriver/StateDrain default to
55	// it; a non-V handoff never consults the scratch GPA, so that is fine, but if
56	// a V handoff reaches the sweep with the GPA still unset the driver throws
57	// (loud) rather than silently transporting V through a bogus address.
58	inline constexpr uint64_t kVScratchGpaUnset =
59	  static_cast<uint64_t>(-1);
60	
61	// GPR block-load prototype: x1..x31 (8 bytes each) staged in the TOP of the
62	// scratch page so the resume ld-sweep reads them below the V region (which
63	// grows up from the base). Reusing the V page keeps this single-repo; it only
64	// applies when the V data leaves room (gpr_scratch_fits), else the caller falls
65	// back to per-register abstract writes. A production version would give the GPR
66	// block its own scratch page instead of sharing the V one.
67	inline constexpr std::size_t kGprScratchBytes = 31 * 8;  // x1..x31
68	
69	inline constexpr auto gpr_scratch_gpa(uint64_t v_scratch_base) -> uint64_t
70	{
71	  return v_scratch_base + kVScratchBytes - kGprScratchBytes;
72	}
73	
74	inline constexpr auto gpr_scratch_fits(uint64_t vlenb) -> bool
75	{
76	  return static_cast<std::size_t>(32) * vlenb <= kVScratchBytes - kGprScratchBytes;
77	}
78	
79	// FPR block-load: f0..f31 (8 bytes each) staged just BELOW the GPR block. Unlike
80	// x0, f0 is a real register, so all 32 f-regs ride the sweep (kFprScratchBytes =
81	// 32*8, not 31*8). The two blocks are disjoint and staged up front, so the FPR
82	// fld-sweep (early in resume) and the GPR ld-sweep (later) never collide. The V
83	// region grows up from the base, so the fit gate here is tighter than the GPR
84	// one -- V must clear both blocks.
85	inline constexpr std::size_t kFprScratchBytes = 32 * 8;  // f0..f31
86	
87	inline constexpr auto fpr_scratch_gpa(uint64_t v_scratch_base) -> uint64_t
88	{
89	  return v_scratch_base + kVScratchBytes - kGprScratchBytes - kFprScratchBytes;
90	}
91	
92	inline constexpr auto fpr_scratch_fits(uint64_t vlenb) -> bool
93	{
94	  return static_cast<std::size_t>(32) * vlenb
95	         <= kVScratchBytes - kGprScratchBytes - kFprScratchBytes;
96	}
97	
98	namespace detail
99	{
100	
101	// Byte offset of the scratch region inside a RAM span: its top page. Throws
102	// if the span is smaller than one scratch page (a too-small RAM mapping).
103	inline auto scratch_offset(std::size_t ram_size) -> std::size_t
104	{
105	  if (ram_size < kVScratchBytes)
106	    throw std::runtime_error(
107	      "v_regfile_xfer: RAM span smaller than the V scratch page");
108	  return ram_size - kVScratchBytes;
109	}
110	
111	}  // namespace detail
112	
113	// Copy state.vreg[] into the span's top scratch page. Called just before vsim
114	// resumes the hart so the fixture can vle8.v from scratch and pick up QEMU 1's
115	// V values.
116	inline void stage_v_to_scratch(const hybrid_state_v1& state,
117	                               std::span<uint8_t> ram)
118	{
119	  const auto off = detail::scratch_offset(ram.size());
120	  // Pack at vlenb stride (drop the wire-format padding) so v0..v31 sit
121	  // contiguously and the Program-Buffer sweep can move 8 at a time via LMUL=8.
122	  const std::size_t vlenb = state.vlenb;
123	  for (std::size_t r = 0; r < 32; ++r)
124	    std::memcpy(ram.data() + off + r * vlenb,
125	                state.vreg + r * HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX, vlenb);
126	}
127	
128	// Pack x1..x31 (8 bytes each) contiguously into the top kGprScratchBytes of the
129	// scratch page; the resume ld-sweep reads them back. state.gpr[1..31] is itself
130	// contiguous, so this is a single memcpy. Called before resume, gated by the
131	// caller on gpr_scratch_fits (the V region must leave room in the page).
132	inline void stage_gpr_to_scratch(const hybrid_state_v1& state,
133	                                 std::span<uint8_t> ram)
134	{
135	  const auto off =
136	    detail::scratch_offset(ram.size()) + (kVScratchBytes - kGprScratchBytes);
137	  std::memcpy(ram.data() + off, &state.gpr[1], 31 * 8);
138	}
139	
140	// Pack f0..f31 (8 bytes each) contiguously into the scratch page just below the
141	// GPR block; the resume fld-sweep reads them back. state.fpr[0..31] is itself
142	// contiguous, so this is a single memcpy. Called before resume, gated by the
143	// caller on fpr_scratch_fits (the V region must leave room for both blocks).
144	inline void stage_fpr_to_scratch(const hybrid_state_v1& state,
145	                                 std::span<uint8_t> ram)
146	{
147	  const auto off = detail::scratch_offset(ram.size())
148	                   + (kVScratchBytes - kGprScratchBytes - kFprScratchBytes);
149	  std::memcpy(ram.data() + off, &state.fpr[0], 32 * 8);
150	}
151	
152	// Copy the span's top scratch page into state.vreg[]. Called inside the vsim
153	// drain path after the fixture's prologue vse8.v has settled the (possibly
154	// mutated) regfile bytes into RAM.
155	inline void read_v_from_scratch(hybrid_state_v1& state,
156	                                std::span<const uint8_t> ram)
157	{
158	  const auto off = detail::scratch_offset(ram.size());
159	  // Unpack the vlenb-packed scratch back into the wire-strided vreg[] slots.
160	  // Each slot's padding (bytes vlenb..HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX) is left as-is:
161	  // callers pass a passthrough state whose padding is already zero (the QEMU
162	  // drain zero-fills it), so the full 128-byte slots stay byte-identical to the
163	  // oracle that --verify compares against.
164	  const std::size_t vlenb = state.vlenb;
165	  for (std::size_t r = 0; r < 32; ++r)
166	    std::memcpy(state.vreg + r * HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX,
167	                ram.data() + off + r * vlenb, vlenb);
168	}
169	
170	}  // namespace hybrid

With the QEMU2 handback removed, the code after your ROI never runs, so a
hybrid run normally proves only that a cycle figure came out. `--verify`
(default OFF) cross-checks the run's correctness:

```sh
./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --verify your_prog.elf
# ...
# [marker window_cycles] 46  (vsim mcycle=... - qemu mcycle=...)
# [state-diff] PASS: 109 fields match (counters and passthrough CSRs excluded)
# [verify] PASS: vsim drain matches the QEMU oracle
```

Performance note: without `--verify`, the vsim leg drains only `mcycle`/`minstret`
(the cycle figure) and skips reading back the full architectural register file
over the Debug Module -- ~190 abstract commands (all FPRs, the vector-register
sweep, the Andes/M-ext CSR blocks) whose simulated debug cycles dominate hybrid
wall-clock for a short ROI but never affect the cycle count. `--verify` needs
every field for the diff, so it keeps the full drain; expect a `--verify` run to
take noticeably longer than the same run without it.

How it works: after the normal run, the same ELF re-runs on pure QEMU (the
oracle) with the plugin draining at the ROI exit boundary, sampled at the
exact pc where vsim halted. The pre-ROI path is QEMU in both runs, so the
ROI inputs are identical -- any architectural divergence inside the ROI
(RTL bug, state-restore bug, drain bug) shows up as a field mismatch and
the run exits non-zero, listing each differing field:

```
[state-diff] x10: ref=0x3d got=0x0
[state-diff] FAIL: 1 mismatch(es) (115 fields compared)
```

What is compared: pc, all GPRs, all FPRs (when FP state is live), the V
CSRs and full vector registers (when V state is live), and the writable
M-mode CSRs that round-trip through the handoff -- `mscratch` (L23) and
`mepc`/`mcause`/`mtval`/`mie` (L24), restored at resume and re-read at
drain. What is not:

- `mcycle`/`minstret` -- the engines count differently by design;
- `mip` -- restored and re-read, but its pending bits are hardware-driven
  (the timer bit tracks elapsed time, which differs between QEMU's
  functional clock and vsim's cycle clock), so a compare would
  false-positive;
- `mstatus`, `mtvec` -- passthrough: vsim restores the QEMU1 entry snapshot value; both sides hold the same bits by construction so comparing is trivially true but not useful;

Performance note: without `--verify`, the vsim leg drains only `mcycle`/`minstret`
(the cycle figure) and skips reading back the full architectural register file
over the Debug Module. The GPR and FPR readback ride Program-Buffer sweeps into

remains of the full drain is mostly the Andes/M-ext CSR blocks and the scalar

## What changed (TDD RED->GREEN, Tidy-First)

**Structural (behavior-preserving, existing tests held green):**
1. `pb_block_load` -> free `pb_block_sweep` in program_buffer.hpp, gains a `last_reg` bound so a store can exclude its base register. GPR/FPR **load and drain** now share one sweep loop (4 call sites). resume_driver 442/442 unchanged.
2. Extracted `StateDrain::halt_and_capture_pc_priv`, shared by `drain()` and `drain_with_passthrough`.

**Behavioral (each its own RED->GREEN):**
3. `encode_sd`/`encode_fsd` - golden hex from `riscv64-elf-as`.
4. `read_gpr_from_scratch`/`read_fpr_from_scratch` - roundtrip-tested against the stage helpers (same offset both directions).
5. `StateDrain::set_gpr_block_store`/`set_fpr_block_store` + gated `sd`/`fsd` sweeps. GPR base x31 is captured via one abstract read and excluded from the sweep (seeding destroys its value); FPR base x5 is already-drained scratch.
6. Simulator wiring: `HandoffController::set_block_store_drain` -> StateDrain; `check_hybrid_handoff` lifts x1..x30 + f0..f31 from scratch, fits-gated exactly like the resume staging.

## Round-trip win (drain side = resume side)

| drain readback | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| GPR | 31 abstract reads | 1 base capture + ~5 `sd` execs = **~6** |
| FPR | 32 abstract reads | 1 seed + ~5 `fsd` execs = **~6** |

~63 -> ~12 round-trips, on every `--verify` drain.

content.text:
The register blocks are done. What's left is all CSRs - and they are a worse PB fit than GPR/FPR/V, so the returns diminish from here.

## What's still on abstract commands (per round-trip each)

| block | resume | drain | when | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PMP** (64 pmpaddr + 8 pmpcfg) | 72 | - | S/U handoffs only | consecutive CSRs, dense; ordering constraint (all addr before cfg) |
| **Andes V5** (13 scalars + 18 PMA) | ~caps subset | ~caps subset | every Andes core | PMA (pmaaddr0..15) consecutive; scalars scattered |
| **M-ext** (~17 on premium) | ~caps subset | ~caps subset | caps-gated | scattered addresses |
| scattered M-mode (mtvec/mscratch/mepc/mcause/mtval/mie/mip, mcache_ctl, mmisc_ctl) | ~9 | ~6 | every handoff | distinct addresses, no run |
| V scalar CSRs, fcsr, DPC, mstatus, counters | ~8 | ~9 | - | small, unavoidable |

## Why CSRs batch worse than registers

A GPR/FPR sweep packs **7 loads per round-trip** - one uniform `ld`, only rd+offset vary. A CSR cannot: the 12-bit CSR number is **baked into the `csrrw` encoding**, not a runtime operand. So each CSR needs `ld xN, off(base); csrrw x0, <csr>, xN` - **2 insns, ~3 CSRs per round-trip**, not 7.

Worse, there is a **fault-isolation** problem. Today each CSR restore is individually tolerant (`write_csr_tolerant` mirrors an unimplemented CSR as a no-op by clearing cmderr). Inside one PB execution you lose that: a single faulting `csrrw` raises cmderr and **kills the rest of the batch**. So a CSR sweep may only carry CSRs the caps say are implemented - which the Andes/M-ext blocks already gate on, but the scattered M-mode ones do not.

## The one clean lever left (altitude, not special-cases)

A **generic staged-CSR PB sweep**: `csr_sweep(bus, base, [(csr,value)...])` - stage values in scratch, emit `ld`+`csrrw` pairs batched at progbufsize-1, reuse for every caps-known block in both directions. That is the right shape (one primitive, not per-block hacks). Apply it to:

1. **Andes V5 + M-ext blocks** - the largest **always-present** consumer on the default engine, both directions. `~caps subset` each -> ~1/3. Best frequency.
2. **PMP block on resume** (72 -> ~24) - biggest single block, but **S/U-only**; the default M-mode engine never takes it.

## Honest recommendation

The high-value PB work is done. GPR+FPR+V were ~190 register moves -> ~36 round-trips (the sweet spot: uniform, large, always-present). The CSR tail is ~120 -> maybe ~45 at 3x, for more code and the fault-isolation caveat above. Real but second-order.

If you want to continue, build the one generic `csr_sweep` and point it at Andes+M-ext first (best frequency). If your workloads never use S/U mode, skip PMP. If they do, PMP is the biggest single win.

content.text:
Two concepts, then your PMP question.

## 1. Andes + M-ext = two groups of CSRs the handoff already carries

Real, existing blocks (dumped above). A bare-metal Andes core sets these up before your ROI, so the handoff must copy them:

- **Andes V5 block** - 13 vendor CSRs (`mxstatus` 0x7C4, `milmb`/`mdlmb` ILM/DLM base, `uitb`, `jvt`, `mhsp_ctl` stack-protect...) plus PMA (2 `pmacfg` + 16 `pmaaddr`, physical-memory attributes). Andes-specific machine setup.
- **M-ext block** - ~30 standard M-mode CSRs (`menvcfg`, `mcounteren`, the perf counters `mhpmcounter3..`, the resumable-NMI save/restore set `mnscratch`/`mnepc`/`msaveepc1`...).

Today each one moves with **one abstract command = one hart round-trip**, restored at resume and re-read at drain, caps-gated (skip what the engine lacks).

## 2. generic csr_sweep = a NEW helper (does not exist yet)

The CSR analog of the `pb_block_sweep` you just built for GPR/FPR. Difference:

- GPR/FPR sweep: **one** uniform insn per register - `ld rd, off(base)`. 7 fit one PB execution.
- CSR sweep: **two** insns per CSR - load the value, then write it:

```
ld    x5, 0(x6)       # value for mxstatus, staged in scratch
csrrw x0, 0x7C4, x5   # mxstatus = x5
ld    x5, 8(x6)
csrrw x0, 0x7C0, x5   # milmb = x5
ld    x5, 16(x6)
csrrw x0, 0x7C1, x5   # mdlmb = x5
ebreak                # 7 slots -> ONE round-trip for 3 CSRs
```

Why two insns: the CSR number (0x7C4) is **baked into the `csrrw` encoding**, not a register operand - so you cannot loop one instruction over many CSRs. `csr_sweep(bus, base, [(csr,value)...])` would stage the values in scratch and emit these `ld`+`csrrw` pairs batched. One helper, reused for any CSR block, both directions.

## Why not choose PMP?

Not because PMP is bad - it is the **biggest single block** (72: 64 `pmpaddr` + 8 `pmpcfg`) and a fine target. I ranked it lower for **one reason: frequency**.

PMP is restored only on **S/U-mode handoffs**. The resume code guards it with `if (state.priv != 3)`:

```
if (state.priv != 3) {          // not M-mode
  for (...) write pmpaddr...    // 64
  for (...) write pmpcfg...     //  8
}
```

The **default engine `ax45mpv_premium` is M-mode-only** (`NDS_NUM_PRIVILEGE_LEVELS=1`), so on the common path PMP is **skipped entirely - 0 round-trips**. It only runs on the S/U-capable `ax66_makatau` engine with the `rt_priv_smode`/`umode` fixtures.

Andes+M-ext, by contrast, fire on **every Andes handoff, both legs** (resume + drain) - and the default engine IS Andes. So batching them speeds up what every run pays.

**The honest tie-breaker is your workload:**
- Bare-metal M-mode benchmarks (what the fixtures mostly are) -> Andes+M-ext is the common-case win; PMP does nothing.
- S/U / OS-level code -> PMP flips to **#1**, biggest single win.

And the key point: the **generic `csr_sweep` is the same code either way**. Build it once; point it at PMP or Andes+M-ext by which block your real workloads exercise. So "which first" only decides where you aim it, not what you build.

Which do your target workloads run - M-mode bare-metal, or S/U?

content.text:
Golden hex confirmed. Here's the architecture, then I start.

## Core architecture (mirrors the GPR/FPR/V pattern you already have)

**Scratch page (4096 B) - add a CSR value region below FPR:**
```
[0 ............ 32*vlenb)   V-data      (grows up)
        ... gap ...
[top-1160 ... top-504)      CSR values  (82 slots x 8B = 656 B)   <- NEW
[top-504 .... top-248)      FPR block   (256 B)
[top-248 .......... top)    GPR block   (248 B)
```
Gate `csr_scratch_fits(vlenb)`: `32*vlenb <= 2936` (VLEN<=512 fits; larger falls back, as GPR/FPR already do).

**The split (same 3 actors as before):**
- Simulator **stages** supported CSR values -> CSR scratch (host memcpy, before resume)
- ResumeDriver **sweeps restore**: per CSR `ld xVAL,(i*8)(base); csrrw x0,addr,xVAL`
- StateDrain **sweeps drain**: per CSR `csrr xVAL,addr; sd xVAL,(i*8)(base)`
- Simulator **lifts** CSR scratch -> state (host memcpy, after drain)

**Why 2 insns/CSR:** the CSR number is baked into `csrrw`/`csrr`, so no uniform loop - ~3 CSRs per PB execution (vs 7 registers). One new encoder needed: `encode_csrrs` (the read); `ld`/`csrrw`/`sd` already exist.

**Decisions (from your TDD/root-cause principles - correct me if wrong):**
1. **Both directions** (restore + drain), like #1.
2. **Include everything** (13 Andes + 18 PMA + 51 M-ext) - "generic" = one mechanism for all 82.
3. **Trust caps, fail loud.** The batch carries only caps-supported CSRs (same gate as today). A faulting batch means caps is wrong = a real config bug to fix, not silently mirror-as-noop. This replaces today's per-CSR tolerant-clear. Risk: I can only run `premium` locally, so the full e2e suite (all 5 engines + S/U) should run before committing.

**Ordering:** stage/sweep/lift each iterate the SAME X-macros + SAME caps -> identical order. Consistent with how plugin/restore/reread/diff already share the X-macro.

## TDD increments

3. `csr_sweep` PB helper (both directions)

6. Simulator stage+lift wiring -> e2e `--verify`

content.text:
dir=1 is Drain. The sweep faults on **`csrr` of mcountermask_m (0x7D1)** — a caps-supported Andes CSR that the abstract DM path reads fine but hart-level `csrr` rejects. And there are likely more past it. This is conclusive: **the caps-supported set is not a reliable predictor of hart csrr/csrrw legality**, and the abstract path's per-CSR tolerance is load-bearing — which a batched PB sweep fundamentally cannot replicate.

This confirms the risk I flagged. The proper call: the CSR PB sweep is **not viable** for the heterogeneous Andes+M-ext blocks without a per-CSR hart-accessibility model (a separate, engine-specific effort). I'll keep the tested primitives but disable the wiring so production stays on the correct abstract path. Reverting debug first:

Done investigating. Honest result: **the CSR sweep works and is fully unit-tested, but e2e proved it cannot ship for Andes+M-ext.** I've disabled the wiring; production stays on the correct abstract path.

## What the e2e caught

A hart `csrr` of **mcountermask_m (0x7D1)** — a CSR premium's own `--describe` advertises as supported — raises **cmderr=3** (illegal instruction) in the Program Buffer. The abstract DM read path reads it fine; the hart's `csrr`/`csrrw` rejects it. And it aborts mid-block, so there are likely more past it.

## Why it's fundamental (not a bug I can patch)

- **caps ≠ hart-accessibility.** The capability set says "the DM can access this CSR," which is *not* the same as "a `csrr`/`csrrw` instruction executing in the hart is legal." The abstract path and the hart-instruction path have different fault semantics for edge CSRs.
- **The abstract path's per-CSR `clear_cmderr` tolerance is load-bearing** — it silently absorbs exactly these faults. A batched PB sweep can't tolerate a mid-batch fault: one bad `csrr` kills the whole `exec_progbuf`.
- This is the "worse fit" I flagged up front — CSRs are heterogeneous and individually tolerant, unlike the uniform, always-legal GPR/FPR/V register moves.

## Current state (all green)

| | result |
|---|---|
| Unit suites (program_buffer 121, v_regfile 298, resume_driver 4217, state_drain 1068, handoff 19) | all pass — the sweep code is fully tested |
| e2e `--verify` rt_all_gprs / rt_all_fprs / rt_c_v_regs | **PASS 146 fields** (abstract path; #1 GPR/FPR drain sweeps still on) |

The full machinery exists behind opt-in flags (default **off**): `encode_csrrs`, `csr_sweep`, the CSR scratch region, `for_each_sweep_csr`, `stage/read_csr`, and the `restore_andes_m_ext`/`drain_andes_m_ext` methods with sweep-or-abstract branches. The simulator simply doesn't enable it, with a comment explaining why.

## Your call

The feature is built and tested but can't be safely enabled. Three ways forward:

Let me explain in very simple words.

## What happened

You asked me to make CSR copying **faster**. (CSR = small setting inside the CPU.)

I built it. All my small tests passed. 

Then I ran it on the **real simulator**. It **crashed**.

## Why it crashed (simple picture)

Think of mailing letters:

- **Old way (slow):** mail one letter at a time. If one address is bad, skip that one, keep going. Safe.
- **New way (fast):** put many letters in one box, mail the box together. If **one** address is bad, the **whole box** is rejected. 

Some CSRs are like a "bad address" - the CPU says **"no"** when I touch them the fast way. The old slow way just skipped them quietly. The new fast way cannot skip - one bad CSR breaks everything.

I found one bad CSR (`mcountermask_m`). There are probably more.

- I **turned OFF** the new fast way.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

1	// Program Buffer execution helpers for the RISC-V Debug Module.
2	//
3	// Follows the same duck-typed template pattern as dmi_poll.hpp so that
4	// resume_driver.hpp can include this header without a circular dependency.
5	// Bus type requirement: write(uint8_t reg, uint32_t val) and
6	//                       read(uint8_t reg) -> uint32_t.
7	//
8	// Debug Spec references: section 3.6 (Program Buffer), table 3.1 (DMI),
9	// section 3.7.1.3 (Abstract Command - Access Register).
10	
11	#pragma once
12	
13	#include "hybrid/abstract_command.hpp"
14	#include "hybrid/dmi_poll.hpp"
15	
16	#include <array>
17	#include <cstdint>
18	#include <span>
19	#include <stdexcept>
20	#include <string>
21	
22	namespace hybrid {
23	
24	// DMI address of the first Program Buffer register (progbuf0..progbuf15).
25	inline constexpr uint8_t kProgbuf0 = 0x20u;
26	
27	// Max payload instructions: 16 total slots minus 1 reserved for the
28	// mandatory ebreak that terminates execution.
29	inline constexpr std::size_t kProgbufMaxInsns = 15u;
30	
31	// Standard ebreak encoding (funct12=1, opcode=SYSTEM).
32	inline constexpr uint32_t kEbreak = 0x00100073u;
33	
34	// "Execute Program Buffer only" command (Debug Spec table 3.1):
35	//   cmdtype  = 0 (Access Register)
36	//   aarsize  = Bits64 (3) - ignored by DM when transfer=0, set for consistency
37	//   postexec = 1 (bit 18)
38	//   transfer = 0 (bit 17 NOT set) - skip register I/O, only run progbuf
39	//   write    = 0 (irrelevant when transfer=0)
40	//   regno    = 0 (irrelevant when transfer=0)
41	inline constexpr uint32_t kExecProgbufCmd =
42	    (uint32_t(AarSize::Bits64) & 0x7u) << 20 | (1u << 18);
43	
44	// Encode `vsetvl rd, rs1, rs2` (RVV 1.0 section 6.2, funct7=1000000).
45	// Tier-B restore: stage vl in rs1 and vtype in rs2 via Abstract Commands,
46	// then branch-free-restore both in one Program Buffer execution.
47	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_vsetvl(uint8_t rd, uint8_t rs1, uint8_t rs2)
48	{
49	    return (0b1000000u << 25)
50	         | ((uint32_t(rs2) & 0x1Fu) << 20)
51	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
52	         | (0b111u << 12)
53	         | ((uint32_t(rd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
54	         | 0x57u;  // OP-V opcode
55	}
56	
57	// Encode `csrrw rd, csr, rs1` (SYSTEM opcode, funct3=001).
58	// Tier-A PB fallback: stage the CSR value in rs1 via Abstract Command,
59	// then write it to a CSR that the DM cannot reach via abstract access.
60	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_csrrw(uint8_t rd, uint16_t csr, uint8_t rs1)
61	{
62	    return ((uint32_t(csr) & 0xFFFu) << 20)
63	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
64	         | (0b001u << 12)
65	         | ((uint32_t(rd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
66	         | 0x73u;  // SYSTEM opcode
67	}
68	
69	// Encode `csrrs rd, csr, rs1` (SYSTEM opcode, funct3=010). With rs1=x0 this is
70	// `csrr rd, csr`: a pure CSR read (the RISC-V spec suppresses the write side
71	// effect when rs1=x0). The CSR drain sweep reads each supported Andes/M-ext CSR
72	// into a temp GPR with this, then sd's it to the scratch page.
73	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_csrrs(uint8_t rd, uint16_t csr, uint8_t rs1)
74	{
75	    return ((uint32_t(csr) & 0xFFFu) << 20)
76	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
77	         | (0b010u << 12)
78	         | ((uint32_t(rd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
79	         | 0x73u;  // SYSTEM opcode
80	}
81	
82	// Encode `vle8.v vd, (rs1)` - unit-stride vector load, EEW=8 (RVV 1.0 sec 7.4).
83	// Fields: vm=1 (unmasked, bit 25), width=000, mop=00, mew=0, nf=000,
84	// lumop=00000, opcode LOAD-FP=0x07. PB V-regfile reload sweeps v0..v31 from
85	// the shared scratch region after a vsetvl to e8/m1.
86	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_vle8_v(uint8_t vd, uint8_t rs1)
87	{
88	    return (1u << 25)
89	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
90	         | ((uint32_t(vd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
91	         | 0x07u;  // LOAD-FP opcode
92	}
93	
94	// Encode `vse8.v vs3, (rs1)` - unit-stride vector store, EEW=8. Mirror of
95	// encode_vle8_v with opcode STORE-FP=0x27. PB V-regfile dump sweeps v0..v31
96	// back to the shared scratch region at drain.
97	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_vse8_v(uint8_t vs3, uint8_t rs1)
98	{
99	    return (1u << 25)
100	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
101	         | ((uint32_t(vs3) & 0x1Fu) << 7)
102	         | 0x27u;  // STORE-FP opcode
103	}
104	
105	// Encode `addi rd, rs1, imm12` (OP-IMM opcode 0x13, funct3=000). The batched
106	// V-data sweep advances the scratch base pointer x7 by one register-span
107	// between transfers WITHIN a Program-Buffer execution, so the per-register
108	// abstract x7 write disappears. imm12 is a signed 12-bit field (-2048..2047).
109	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_addi(uint8_t rd, uint8_t rs1, int32_t imm12)
110	{
111	    return ((uint32_t(imm12) & 0xFFFu) << 20)
112	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
113	         | ((uint32_t(rd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
114	         | 0x13u;  // OP-IMM opcode (funct3=000)
115	}
116	
117	// Encode `ld rd, imm12(rs1)` (LOAD opcode 0x03, funct3=011 for 64-bit). The GPR
118	// block-load sweeps x1..x31 from a scratch region addressed by a base register,
119	// so 31 abstract register writes collapse into a few Program-Buffer executions.
120	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_ld(uint8_t rd, uint8_t rs1, int32_t imm12)
121	{
122	    return ((uint32_t(imm12) & 0xFFFu) << 20)
123	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
124	         | (0b011u << 12)
125	         | ((uint32_t(rd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
126	         | 0x03u;  // LOAD opcode
127	}
128	
129	// Encode `fld rd, imm12(rs1)` (LOAD-FP opcode 0x07, funct3=011 for double). Same
130	// shape as encode_ld with the FP-load opcode: the FPR block-load sweeps f0..f31
131	// from the scratch region via an integer base register, collapsing 32 abstract
132	// FPR writes into a few Program-Buffer executions.
133	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_fld(uint8_t rd, uint8_t rs1, int32_t imm12)
134	{
135	    return ((uint32_t(imm12) & 0xFFFu) << 20)
136	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
137	         | (0b011u << 12)
138	         | ((uint32_t(rd)  & 0x1Fu) << 7)
139	         | 0x07u;  // LOAD-FP opcode
140	}
141	
142	// Encode `sd rs2, imm12(rs1)` (STORE opcode 0x23, funct3=011 for 64-bit). The
143	// mirror of encode_ld for the DRAIN direction: the GPR drain sweeps x1..x30 from
144	// the regfile INTO the scratch region via an integer base register, collapsing
145	// 31 abstract reads into a few Program-Buffer executions. S-type splits the
146	// signed 12-bit immediate: imm[11:5] -> bits 31:25, imm[4:0] -> bits 11:7.
147	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_sd(uint8_t rs2, uint8_t rs1, int32_t imm12)
148	{
149	    const uint32_t imm = uint32_t(imm12) & 0xFFFu;
150	    return ((imm >> 5) & 0x7Fu) << 25
151	         | ((uint32_t(rs2) & 0x1Fu) << 20)
152	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
153	         | (0b011u << 12)
154	         | ((imm & 0x1Fu) << 7)
155	         | 0x23u;  // STORE opcode
156	}
157	
158	// Encode `fsd rs2, imm12(rs1)` (STORE-FP opcode 0x27, funct3=011 for double).
159	// Same S-type shape as encode_sd with the FP-store opcode: the FPR drain sweeps
160	// f0..f31 from the regfile into the scratch region via an integer base register.
161	inline constexpr uint32_t encode_fsd(uint8_t rs2, uint8_t rs1, int32_t imm12)
162	{
163	    const uint32_t imm = uint32_t(imm12) & 0xFFFu;
164	    return ((imm >> 5) & 0x7Fu) << 25
165	         | ((uint32_t(rs2) & 0x1Fu) << 20)
166	         | ((uint32_t(rs1) & 0x1Fu) << 15)
167	         | (0b011u << 12)
168	         | ((imm & 0x1Fu) << 7)
169	         | 0x27u;  // STORE-FP opcode
170	}
171	
172	// Write insns[0..n-1] to progbuf0..n-1 and kEbreak to progbuf[n].
173	// Clears any sticky abstractcs.cmderr (W1C), issues kExecProgbufCmd, polls
174	// until abstractcs.busy clears, then verifies cmderr stayed clear.
175	//
176	// Throws std::runtime_error if insns.size() > kProgbufMaxInsns, if the poll
177	// times out, or if the DM raises cmderr during execution. No caller has a
178	// legitimate reason to silently continue on PB failure - the hart state
179	// would be partially restored / partially drained, which is worse than
180	// surfacing the fault.
181	template<typename Bus>
182	inline void exec_progbuf(Bus& bus, std::span<const uint32_t> insns)
183	{
184	    if (insns.size() > kProgbufMaxInsns)
185	        throw std::runtime_error(
186	            "exec_progbuf: too many instructions ("
187	            + std::to_string(insns.size()) + " > "
188	            + std::to_string(kProgbufMaxInsns) + ")");
189	
190	    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < insns.size(); ++i)
191	        bus.write(static_cast<uint8_t>(kProgbuf0 + i), insns[i]);
192	    bus.write(static_cast<uint8_t>(kProgbuf0 + insns.size()), kEbreak);
193	
194	    if ((bus.read(kDmiAbstractcs) & kAbstractcsCmderrMask) != 0u)
195	        bus.write(kDmiAbstractcs, kAbstractcsCmderrMask);
196	
197	    bus.write(kDmiCommand, kExecProgbufCmd);
198	    poll_until_clear(bus, kDmiAbstractcs, kAbstractcsBusy, "exec_progbuf busy");
199	
200	    const uint32_t cmderr = bus.read(kDmiAbstractcs) & kAbstractcsCmderrMask;
201	    if (cmderr != 0u)
202	        throw std::runtime_error(
203	            "exec_progbuf: PB execution raised cmderr="
204	            + std::to_string(cmderr >> 8));
205	}
206	
207	// vtype encoding for e8, m8, ta, ma (vsew=000, vlmul=011, vta=1, vma=1). The
208	// V-data sweep uses LMUL=8 so one vle8.v/vse8.v moves a whole group of 8
209	// registers (8*vlenb byte-elements, vl=8*vlenb) in a single instruction.
210	inline constexpr uint32_t kVtypeE8M8 = 0xC3u;
211	
212	// Abstract-command write of a 64-bit value to Debug Module register `regno`
213	// (GPR/CSR/FPR): DATA0/DATA1 + Access-Register(write) + busy-poll. Free
214	// function so ResumeDriver, StateDrain, and the V-data sweep share one copy.
215	template<typename Bus>
216	inline void write_register_abstract(Bus& bus, uint16_t regno, uint64_t value)
217	{
218	    bus.write(kDmiData0, static_cast<uint32_t>(value & 0xffffffffu));
219	    bus.write(kDmiData1, static_cast<uint32_t>((value >> 32) & 0xffffffffu));
220	    bus.write(kDmiCommand,
221	              access_register_command(regno, AarSize::Bits64, /*write=*/true));
222	    poll_until_clear(bus, kDmiAbstractcs, kAbstractcsBusy,
223	                     "write_register_abstract");
224	}
225	
226	// Program-Buffer block sweep: seed integer base register `base_gpr` with
227	// `base_gpa`, then run `encode(reg, base_gpr, (reg-first_reg)*8)` for reg in
228	// [first_reg, last_reg) through the Program Buffer, batched at (progbufsize-1)
229	// instructions per execution (one slot reserved for the terminating ebreak).
230	// One uniform load/store encoder drives it, so the GPR/FPR restore (ld/fld,
231	// scratch -> regfile) and the GPR/FPR drain (sd/fsd, regfile -> scratch) share
232	// one implementation: ~32 registers move in ~6 halted-hart round-trips instead
233	// of ~32 abstract commands, and the values ride the shared scratch page, not
234	// DMI. The 8-byte-strided offset spans every slot (<= 248, within ld/sd's
235	// signed 12-bit immediate). The caller guarantees base_gpr is safe to seed: on
236	// a load it may be a swept register that rides LAST (its own load runs after
237	// every other use of it as the base); on a store it must be EXCLUDED from
238	// [first_reg, last_reg) -- seeding destroys its value before it could be stored
239	// -- and captured separately.
240	template<typename Bus>
241	inline void pb_block_sweep(Bus& bus, uint8_t base_gpr, uint64_t base_gpa,
242	                           uint8_t first_reg, uint8_t last_reg,
243	                           uint32_t (*encode)(uint8_t, uint8_t, int32_t))
244	{
245	    // The Program Buffer holds abstractcs.progbufsize entries (this DM reports
246	    // 8); reserve one slot for the terminating ebreak, so at most progbufsize-1
247	    // load/store insns per execution.
248	    const uint32_t progbufsize = (bus.read(kDmiAbstractcs) >> 24) & 0x1Fu;
249	    const std::size_t max_ops = (progbufsize > 1) ? progbufsize - 1u : 1u;
250	    write_register_abstract(bus, regno_gpr(base_gpr), base_gpa);  // base pointer
251	    std::array<uint32_t, 32> batch{};
252	    std::size_t n = 0;
253	    for (uint8_t k = first_reg; k < last_reg; ++k) {
254	        batch[n++] = encode(k, base_gpr,
255	                            static_cast<int32_t>((k - first_reg) * 8));
256	        if (n == max_ops || k + 1 == last_reg) {
257	            exec_progbuf(bus, std::span<const uint32_t>{batch.data(), n});
258	            n = 0;
259	        }
260	    }
261	}
262	
263	// Direction for csr_sweep: Restore writes each CSR from the scratch page
264	// (ld + csrrw), Drain reads each CSR back to scratch (csrr + sd).
265	enum class CsrSweepDir { Restore, Drain };
266	
267	// Program-Buffer CSR sweep: transport a caps-supported list of CSRs between the
268	// hart and the scratch page. Unlike pb_block_sweep (one uniform ld/st per
269	// register), a CSR needs TWO instructions -- the CSR number is baked into the
270	// csrrw/csrr immediate, so it cannot be a runtime operand -- so this batches at
271	// (progbufsize-1)/2 CSRs per Program-Buffer execution:
272	//   Restore: ld val,(k*8)(base); csrrw x0, csrs[k], val   (scratch -> CSR)
273	//   Drain:   csrr val, csrs[k];  sd val,(k*8)(base)       (CSR -> scratch)
274	// `base` is an integer GPR seeded once with `base_gpa` (the CSR scratch region);
275	// `val` is a temp GPR the caller may clobber. The values ride the shared scratch
276	// page (staged/lifted by stage_csr_to_scratch / read_csr_from_scratch), not DMI.
277	// The csrs list is the caps-supported set in the SAME canonical order the host
278	// stager packs, so slot k*8 holds csrs[k]'s value. Empty list -> no-op (not even
279	// the base seed). The k*8 offset spans every slot (<= 81*8 = 648 < 2047).
280	//
281	// Every csrs[k] MUST be implemented by the target (the caller builds the list
282	// from caps): a csrrw/csrr to an unimplemented CSR raises cmderr and exec_progbuf
283	// throws, aborting the whole batch. That is intentional -- a faulting sweep means
284	// the caps map is wrong, a config bug to fix, not something to silently mirror.
285	template<typename Bus>
286	inline void csr_sweep(Bus& bus, uint8_t base_gpr, uint64_t base_gpa,
287	                      uint8_t val_gpr, std::span<const uint16_t> csrs,
288	                      CsrSweepDir dir)
289	{
290	    if (csrs.empty()) return;
291	    const uint32_t progbufsize = (bus.read(kDmiAbstractcs) >> 24) & 0x1Fu;
292	    // Two insns per CSR; reserve one slot for the terminating ebreak. Clamp to
293	    // the ebreak-adjusted payload cap so a batch never overruns the buffer.
294	    std::size_t usable = (progbufsize > 1) ? progbufsize - 1u : 1u;
295	    if (usable > kProgbufMaxInsns) usable = kProgbufMaxInsns;
296	    const std::size_t max_csrs = (usable >= 2) ? usable / 2u : 1u;
297	    write_register_abstract(bus, regno_gpr(base_gpr), base_gpa);  // scratch base
298	    std::array<uint32_t, 32> batch{};
299	    std::size_t n = 0, in_batch = 0;
300	    for (std::size_t k = 0; k < csrs.size(); ++k) {
301	        const int32_t off = static_cast<int32_t>(k * 8);
302	        if (dir == CsrSweepDir::Restore) {
303	            batch[n++] = encode_ld(val_gpr, base_gpr, off);
304	            batch[n++] = encode_csrrw(0, csrs[k], val_gpr);
305	        } else {
306	            batch[n++] = encode_csrrs(val_gpr, csrs[k], 0);
307	            batch[n++] = encode_sd(val_gpr, base_gpr, off);
308	        }
309	        if (++in_batch == max_csrs || k + 1 == csrs.size()) {
310	            exec_progbuf(bus, std::span<const uint32_t>{batch.data(), n});
311	            n = 0;
312	            in_batch = 0;
313	        }
314	    }
315	}
316	
317	// Sweep all 32 V data registers between the hart regfile and the vlenb-packed
318	// scratch region via the Program Buffer. load=true issues vle8.v
319	// (scratch -> regfile, on resume); load=false issues vse8.v (regfile ->
320	// scratch, at drain). The leading vsetvl to e8/m8 sets vl=8*vlenb and forces
321	// vstart=0, so one unit-stride access covers a whole LMUL=8 group of 8
322	// registers. Uses x5/x6 (vsetvl operands) and x7 (group base pointer) as
323	// scratch. `vlenb` is the runtime per-register width; the scratch must be
324	// packed at vlenb stride (stage_v_to_scratch) so each 8-register group is
325	// contiguous.
326	template<typename Bus>
327	inline void pb_v_data_sweep(Bus& bus, uint64_t scratch_gpa, uint64_t vlenb,
328	                            bool load)
329	{
330	    // The scratch holds v0..v31 packed contiguously at vlenb stride (see
331	    // stage_v_to_scratch), so 8 consecutive registers form one LMUL=8 group.
332	    // One vle8.v/vse8.v then moves a whole group (8*vlenb contiguous bytes,
333	    // vl=8*vlenb) and all 32 registers transfer in 4 grouped ops -- whose 4
334	    // (transfer; addi) pairs fit in a SINGLE Program-Buffer execution. Each PB
335	    // execution is one halted-hart DM round-trip (~1000 sim cycles in the
336	    // busy-poll), so this is the floor: one vsetvl + one grouped execution. The
337	    // register bytes never cross DMI; they ride the shared mmap.
338	    constexpr unsigned     kRegsPerGroup   = 8;  // LMUL=8
339	    // kVtypeE8M8's vlmul field (bits 2:0) must encode this LMUL, so one grouped
340	    // vle8.v/vse8.v really covers kRegsPerGroup registers (integer LMUL=1<<vlmul;
341	    // 0xC3 & 7 == 3 -> LMUL 8).
342	    static_assert((1u << (kVtypeE8M8 & 0x7u)) == kRegsPerGroup,
343	                  "kVtypeE8M8 must encode LMUL = kRegsPerGroup");
344	    constexpr std::size_t  kGroupSweepInsns = (32 / kRegsPerGroup) * 2;  // (ld;addi)*4
345	    static_assert(kGroupSweepInsns <= kProgbufMaxInsns,
346	                  "the grouped sweep must fit one Program Buffer execution");
347	    const uint64_t group_bytes = static_cast<uint64_t>(kRegsPerGroup) * vlenb;
348	    if (group_bytes > 2047)  // addi imm12 is signed 12-bit; max 8*128 = 1024
349	        throw std::runtime_error(
350	            "pb_v_data_sweep: 8*vlenb exceeds the addi imm12 range");
351	
352	    // vsetvl to e8/m8 with AVL = 8*vlenb sets vl = VLMAX = 8*vlenb (one
353	    // byte-element per lane across the whole group) and forces vstart = 0.
354	    write_register_abstract(bus, regno_gpr(5), group_bytes);  // AVL

=== Stack protection ordering (msp_base/msp_bound/mhsp_ctl) ~line 1015-1035 ===
Top of Stack Recording
The top of stack recording scheme records the top of stack boundary by comparing the updated value
to the SP register (via any instruction) with the value of the stack bound register. If the updated value
to the SP register is smaller than the value of the stack bound register, the stack bound register is
revised with the updated value in SP.
2.3
Control of the Mechanism
Before enabling this mechanism, one should ﬁrst select the operating scheme and the usage mode of
the mechanism. The “usage mode(s)” include a machine mode bit, a supervisor mode bit, and a user
mode bit.
To use the mechanism properly, one can initialize the stack pointer register, the msp_bound and the
msp_base registers before enabling the mechanism. When the mechanism is already in operation,
if one wants to switch to another task stack, one should change or initialize the msp_bound and the
msp_base registers ﬁrst before changing the stack pointer register. Following this update sequence
avoids an unexpected Stack Overﬂow/Underﬂow Exception in the stack range protection scheme and
makes sure a proper setup in the top of stack recording scheme. This update sequence works because
the msp_bound/msp_base registers are only compared on a stack pointer register update, rather
than being compared all the time. Example codes are provided in Figure 1 and Figure 2 for the two
schemes in this mechanism.
lw a3, msp_bound_offset(a5)   // load new msp_bound value
csrw msp_bound, a3            // update msp_bound register

content.text:
Confirmed, airtight. Here is the answer.

## First, honest: I had NOT read that PDF before. I read the relevant parts now.

Yes - the doc has CSR rules. Two kinds:
1. **"exists only if..."** rules (the doc calls them `IM Requirement`). 154 CSRs have one.
2. **"set in this order"** rules (real ordering dependencies).

Your crash is kind #1. Your ordering question is kind #2. Both are real. Here they are.

## Why `0x7D1` crashed - it is an "exists only if" rule

The doc, page 326, `mcountermask_m` (0x7D1):
> IM Requirement: `mmsc_cfg.PMNDS==1 & misa[20]==1 (User mode implemented)`

So this CSR **exists only if the CPU has User mode.** Now premium's real config:

| premium `config.inc` | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `NDS_NUM_PRIVILEGE_LEVELS` | **1** | M-mode only, **no User mode** |
| `NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT` | 1 | has perf monitor |

No User mode -> `mcountermask_m` **does not exist** on premium -> any read/write is illegal -> `cmderr=3`. Not a mystery. The doc predicted it.

## The exact code bug (one wrong line)

`src/hybrid/andes_caps.hpp`:
```
case 0x7D1: return AndesGate::PERF_MONITOR;   // mcountermask_m   <-- checks perf-monitor ONLY
case ...0x7D3: return AndesGate::UMODE;        // mcountermask_u   <-- checks User mode (correct)
```
`0x7D1` and `0x7D3` are twins - the doc gives **both** the same requirement (PMNDS **and** User mode). But `0x7D1` is tagged "perf-monitor only", so `caps` wrongly says premium has it. `PERF_MONITOR` is set by `NDS_PERFORMANCE_MONITOR_INT=1`, which never checks User mode.

## This changes my earlier answer

Before I told you "the fast sweep hit a wall, cannot ship." That was **too pessimistic**. It did not hit a wall. It hit **one wrong row** in the caps table. Fix the row -> the sweep skips `0x7D1` on premium -> no crash. (A full audit may find a few more wrong rows; each is a small doc-checked fix, not a wall.)

## The ordering rules you asked about (real, touching CSRs we move)

| Rule (from the doc) | CSRs | What order |
|---|---|---|
| Counter write-enable | `mcounterwen` gates `cycle/instret/mcountermask_*/...` | set the enable **first**, else the write is illegal |
| Stack protection (p.14) | `msp_bound`, `msp_base`, `mhsp_ctl` | set bound+base **first**, **then** enable `mhsp_ctl` |
| PMA / PMP | `pmaaddr` / `pmacfg` | all addr **before** cfg (code already does this) |

## Hidden risk this exposes

The old slow path uses `write_csr_tolerant` = "try, ignore the error, move on." So a wrong-existence or wrong-order CSR is **silently skipped**, and `--verify` does not compare it. Meaning: we may not truly be restoring some CSRs **today**, and it is hidden. The fast sweep is actually more honest - it crashes instead of hiding.

## Proposed proper fix (root cause, TDD)

1. **RED**: write a caps test - on an M-only config, `supports_csr(0x7D1)` must be `false`. Today it returns `true`, so the test fails.
2. **GREEN**: fix the gate so `0x7D1` needs perf-monitor **AND** User mode.
3. Audit the other transported CSRs against the doc `IM Requirement`; fix any other wrong rows.
4. Add the two ordering rules (`mcounterwen` before counters; bound/base before `mhsp_ctl`).
5. Re-enable the sweep, re-test e2e.

Want me to start with step 1 - the failing caps test plus the one-line gate fix?
